story: The Monongahela Incline opened on May 28, 1870, and it was the first incline built for carrying passengers. German immigrants had crowded into Pittsburgh for factory jobs, and the only space left was on the steep hills. Prussian-born engineer John Endres designed it, with help from his daughter Caroline, one of the first women engineers in the United States.
On opening day, 944 fares were collected. On the second day, 4,174 people rode it. Each car carries 23 passengers up a track 635 feet long, climbing about 369 feet at a grade of roughly 35 degrees.

Steam power gave way to electricity in 1935. It is the oldest continuously operating funicular in the United States, and one of only two survivors of the 17 passenger inclines Pittsburgh once had. The other is the nearby Duquesne Incline.
stops.fact: It was the first passenger incline in the city.
stops.disputed: Many people say the Duquesne Incline is the oldest. Wikipedia says the Monongahela Incline, from 1870, is the oldest continuously operating funicular in the US.

claims.t: Pittsburgh still has all 17 of its original passenger inclines.
claims.why: Only two survive: the Monongahela and the Duquesne.

spot.why: It was the first incline built for carrying passengers. German immigrants had crowded into Pittsburgh for factory jobs, and the only space left was on the steep hills.

story: The present bridge opened on March 19, 1883, and it was designed by Gustav Lindenthal, who later designed the Hell Gate Bridge in New York City. It is the third bridge on this spot. A wooden bridge from 1818 burned in the Great Fire of 1845, and a wire-rope suspension bridge by John Roebling came next.
The Lindenthal bridge reused the stone piers from Roebling's bridge. It was widened in 1889 and again in 1911, and it is the second-oldest steel bridge in the United States.
Streetcars crossed it until July 1985. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1976, after officials considered replacing it with a modern bridge.
stops.fact: It is built on the piers of an earlier bridge.
stops.disputed: Many people think the first Pittsburgh bridges were steel. Wikipedia says the first bridge here was wooden, from 1818.

claims.t: The Smithfield Street Bridge opened in 1883.
John Roebling designed the bridge that stands today.
claims.why: Roebling built the earlier suspension bridge. Gustav Lindenthal designed the present one.

spot.why: A wooden bridge from 1818 burned in the Great Fire of 1845. A wire-rope suspension bridge by John Roebling came next, and the 1883 bridge reused its stone piers.

story: The earlier courthouse, a Greek Revival building finished in 1841, burned on May 7, 1882. The county held a design competition, and Boston architect Henry Hobson Richardson won it. The Norcross Brothers began construction, and the cornerstone was laid on October 13, 1884.

The building was completed in 1888. It is arranged around an open courtyard that lets light and air reach most of the building, with a five-story tower rising from the courtyard's open side. A covered walkway known as the Bridge of Sighs links it to the old jail.
It is one of the finest examples of Romanesque Revival architecture. Richardson called it his "great achievement", and it became a National Historic Landmark in 1976.
stops.fact: The county held a contest to design it.
stops.disputed: Many people think the courthouse was always on Grant Street. Wikipedia says the first Allegheny County courthouse was a wooden building at Market Square, first used in 1794.

stops.teaser: A small fort building from 1764, the oldest standing structure in western Pennsylvania.
stops.map: Fort Pitt Block House, Point State Park, Pittsburgh, PA

stops.safety: The park is open and busy, with paths shared by walkers and bikes. Check opening hours before you go, and stay off the building's walls.

story: The Block House was built in 1764 as a redoubt, a small defensive fort, for Fort Pitt. Henry Bouquet started building a few of them around the fort's outer walls, and this is the only one that survives.

After the army left, Isaac Craig turned it into a house in 1785. That saved it when Fort Pitt itself was torn down in 1792. In 1894, Mary Schenley gave the deed to the Daughters of the American Revolution.

In 1902, industrialist Henry Clay Frick bought all the land around it and offered the Daughters $25,000 to move it. They refused, and after a long court fight the Pennsylvania Supreme Court sided with them and the Block House stayed put.
stops.fact: It survived because someone turned it into a house.
stops.disputed: Many people think the Block House is part of the original fort walls. Wikipedia says it was a separate redoubt built outside them in 1764.

claims.t: The Block House was built in 1764.
claims.why: Wikipedia: constructed in 1764 as a redoubt of Fort Pitt.

claims.t: Henry Clay Frick moved the Block House to Schenley Park.

spot.why: The Daughters refused, and after a long court fight the Pennsylvania Supreme Court sided with them. The Block House stayed put.
